utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very good morning, everybody. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the same procedure as usual, appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, with Ruth Karper, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we turn to today's witness, when reading yesterday's and the day before's transcript, I suddenly was aware that we indeed discussed the question of the source of the documents presented by the Office of the Prosecutor, being the basis for the search in the cell unit of Dr. Stakic. We discussed this issue in the 65 ter (i) meeting, but it is not yet on the transcript. So therefore, I would kindly ask the OTP to give the explanation where these documents were found to the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the documents, and for the record, that document exhibit number, the eight pages, I'll give that in a moment. Those pages were part of several items that were seized at the time of the arrest of the accused. The accused, Dr. Stakic, was actually arrested by the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He was turned over to representatives of the OTP. At the time that he was turned over, his personal items that were in his possession were also turned over. Photocopies were made of those personal items. One was a phone book type of document, agenda type of document. They totalled 81 pages. Among those 81 pages were the eight pages that are in S - maybe it's seven pages - excuse me, eight pages in S220 to S226. One is a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification to the record. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't also indicate that those eight pages, I believe I said on the record before, but just to be clear, when the items came to the Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor photocopied the items, including the agenda book. That totalled the 81 pages. And the items themselves were turned over to the Office of Legal Aid and Defence, OLAD. I'm not sure what it stands for exactly. Legal Aid and Detention, I believe. And then later I believe I stated for the record that we found out the day of the seizure they indicated that they had records that had been turned over to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, thank you. Any observations by the Defence as regards this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour. Thank you, and good morning. With respect to that, we think that there has to -- especially a criminal proceeding such as this, there has to be at least some chain of custody that would have to be established with respect to the OTP's contention, (A), that the documents were returned to Dr. Stakic, and the chain of custody from when the documents were actually seized from Dr. Stakic. To this date, we have not been provided, nor do I believe there is in existence, any written protocol for setting forth the proper procedure once those documents are taken, to whom do they go, who is the individual who takes custody of those documents, et cetera. Our biggest concern in light of what transpired yesterday and the day before is that there may be an improper and inappropriate inference that would be drawn from those documents, since the Court has already reviewed photocopies of those documents which I believe the OTP has suggested would not be as beneficial, would not be beneficial to their handwriting expert. That we'll see, obviously, once they make their evaluation and opinions based on that. Chain of command, as the panel knows and the Honourable Judges know, is -- chain of custody is extremely important when we're dealing with evidentiary matters such as evidence that was taken from a witness or is directly related or alleged to be something that the witness personally and arguably can expose them to any criminal action. Inferences drawn from that, likewise, are very critical. So I would ask, and I hope to ask later possibly in written form as well, that the exhibit not be permitted into evidence, as I had yesterday, and also that any inferences would not be drawn from those exhibits. Again, we're speaking perhaps a little prematurely because we don't know what the expert's opinion will be in this regard. However, I think thus far it has been clearly established that the chain of custody has not been one that can be accorded under any criminal jurisdiction anywhere in the world where a person, once he's incarcerated, the people from allegedly the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, take the documents, to whom did they give those documents? Then the procedure thereafter, once he was incarcerated and detained here at the United Nations at the ICTY, at the Detention Unit, I'm troubled by the fact that the OTP continues to insist, although only verbally, that the documents were returned to Dr. Stakic. There has been no evidence of that whatsoever. We've consulted with our client on that matter. We would like to establish who actually at the OLAD or any other unit of the OTP, including the OTP offices, who actually sets that claim forth and what's the basis for that claim. And I'm confident, if they did it properly within their procedures, that they would have obtained a receipt from Dr. Stakic in connection with those documents. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, until now, I think none of the parties would say that we have to discuss something like the fruit of poisoned tree doctrine to be applicable in this case. On the other hand, I would appreciate if we could get some documentation when the documents were taken from Dr. Stakic - maybe there is indeed a document indicating what happened during the arrest - and on the other hand, when the documents were transferred to the OLAD, and maybe within the OLAD, there one can find the document how they were forwarded to Dr. Stakic. I think it's in the interest of both parties to find these documents, if possible. On the other hand, we have to emphasise that we, in addition to that, would feel more comfortable when we could find out about the reasons why the search and seizure ordered by this Trial Chamber was not conducted in a proper way and deviated from the order evidently conducted by representatives of the United Nations Detention Unit. I think it's necessary to find some clarification on this issue. Having learned this lesson several times, I would appreciate this, if this dispute could be settled before the Court recess. You wanted to make any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, other than what we need apparently is -- all that Your Honour is asking is in the possession of the OLAD unit, and I guess they are under the Registrar. We will attempt to get that information from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And about the conduct of the order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Again, the Office of the Prosecution was not present. We were contacting them at the time to arrange for an investigator. I asked for an investigator to go there and to clarify how exactly this search was going to be conducted. And then we found out it had already been conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we need some additional clarification in writing for the documents in this case, how this was possible, and who within the United Nations Detention Unit took the liberty to act ex officio, because in this case, fortunately, there was no problem emanating from this for Dr. Stakic. But it could have been the other way around if it was conducted in this unprofessional way. Therefore, some clarification is needed as a matter of principle. Thank you. Today, we'll hear, first of all, the witness. The witness will be cross-examined. Do you believe we come to Madam Tabeau today? What's your impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My impression is yes. I think there's about a half hour or so, 45 minutes, of direct examination remaining. It depends, obviously, on the cross-examination. Perhaps, Your Honour, to be honest, I think Ms. Tabeau is going to be a very short witness. Mr. Inayat, who could testify at any time, but I could call him because we don't have any other witnesses this week. I basically have about two questions on direct. We have a list 6. He will simply testify on direct that lists 4, 5, and 6, that the sourcing column where the documents came from was prepared by him and is accurate, and then we will turn him over for the cross-examination. I think that we have time this week to have the people who know the answers to the questions Your Honour just asked here, if you'd like, I can try to arrange that for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be kind enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We could put off Mr. Inayat also, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I have the impression Mr. Inayat will be cross-examined in depth by the Defence, if I understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly would like the opportunity to discuss with Mr. Inayat some of his procedures and processes that he uses while being an investigator here with the OTP, particularly in connection with this case. However, we do -- and we expect to proceed in an accordingly expeditious fashion. However, the schedule has changed, quite frankly, rather dramatically from what it was commencing last Monday. We don't have a problem with the OTP presenting witnesses in such a fashion; however, it is causing an undue burden on the Defence in order to have scheduled these witnesses and to prepare an adequate defence. Quite frankly, I'd like, if I may, with the Court's permission, to reserve my right to cross-examine Mr. Inayat at a later time since he is readily available at all times. And respectfully to the OTP, there may come an occasion later in their case that there may be some vacancy that we could fill his time with. Similarly with respect to Miss Tabeau or Madam Tabeau, we received her report today, quite frankly, this morning. We had received yesterday transcripts on a case that she testified in, in another courtroom. Actually, it was in this courtroom, just during a different session. We did receive on Monday a report that apparently was not directly related to the case before the Chamber. I am prepared to question Madam Tabeau on some preliminary issues in connection with both the methodology, the source material, the reliability, and some of her background as a demographer in that regard. Perhaps that would be enough. It all depends on the answers that I elicit from her. But I just want the Court to be advised that we are being placed in a position that is unnecessarily overly burdensome on the Defence, and there's no need for that. We were supposed to, as the Court knows, commence Monday morning's session initially with Mr. Mayhew, and we started him last week and concluded him last week. And we were only supposed to have two witnesses this week and two witnesses next week. If I can ask the Court to have the OTP indulge us and to just share with us or enlighten us on a little more accuracy with respect to the witnesses, I can assure the Court we wouldn't ask for an extension with respect to witnesses such as Mr. Inayat, but we'll proceed in accordance with whichever manner the Court suggests to us. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: With all due respect, to a certain respect, I can't understand this contribution because, first, Mr. Inayat was due already two weeks ago and only for purposes -- for unforeseeable reasons, we were not able to hear Mr. Inayat. It was already delayed for the purpose that you, Mr. Ostojic, were present, on the request of Mr. Lukic we delayed the hearing of Mr. Inayat. And therefore, we can expect that you're prepared to cross-examine this witness due since a longer period of time. As regards Madam Tabeau, I'm fully aware that this witness was heard but on totally different circumstances in another case, on Sarajevo. And this document, the underlying document on the population changes in Prijedor from 1991 to 1997, was provided to all of us, I think, two or three weeks ago. So, therefore, there's nothing wrong with this to hear this witness today. Nevertheless, we have only four -- we have tomorrow and then four days next week. I understand that on Thursday next week, there will be the videoconference. Is this still true, that it's the 1st of August? And the last information we got is to do this next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think we confirmed that just yesterday or the day before that it is the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That would be Thursday. And we have -- I want to recall, the entire day of Thursday, therefore nothing on Friday next week, the morning session and afternoon session in Courtroom I. Then there were some rumours in the corridors saying that there would be the line-up somewhere next week. Is this correct? Is it prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the witness is scheduled for Monday. So obviously the witness would have to -- the line-up would have to be at the beginning of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask carefully whether the parties have agreed on an additional four persons to be presented for the line-up?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have not been provided with that information, Your Honour. So there is no agreement in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore I want to ask the parties to come together on this issue, that we don't have any surprise next Monday. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just say for the record that we would include anyone the Defence suggests, but we will give them the people that have agreed that we have contacted. I don't know how to give them to them. I can give them the names, and obviously they may or may not have seen them before. They work in various parts of this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's a matter to be resolved between the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. parties. And secondly, I recall that the Defence didn't agree with the tableau in showing the photographs of other persons. It's already some months ago we were presented with such a table, but apparently there were, as regards two or three persons on this table, there were some problems. And I would ask the parties also on this issue to confer and to come to some solution; otherwise, it has to be resolved with the assistance of this Trial Chamber this week. Then we have, in conclusion, already covered two days of next week. What else can we expect next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think we have those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think the one witness is expected to take several days.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, I have it, but far away from me. Any additional issues before we continue with the examination-in-chief? I can't see any. The usher may bring in the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak, you can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then may I ask Mr. Koumjian to proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Koumjian: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Poljak, when we finished yesterday, you indicated that you were in one room with your father for a month or a month and-a-half. What room was that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a room in the largest building in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You said that your father was called out many times for questioning, and beaten. And that one day, they called him out around 5.00. What happened when your father came back?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came back at about midnight. Most of the people in the room were sleeping. He sat down. He didn't say anything much. He was very scared. You could tell that he was scared by the look of him. He was sweating, but he didn't want to talk about it. He just said: "It's all right. It's all right. It's swell. They didn't hit me. Please, don't lose any sleep over me." And I kept asking him: "Where were you? What did you do? What did they do?" He said it wasn't anything particularly awful. They asked him about the shoe size he was wearing, the size of his clothes, how tall exactly he was. And while they were there, Mr. Brk came along. I knew him as Brk. I know that he used to be a taxi driver, and apparently obviously he knew my father. They were, then, in the white house. The building was referred to as "the white house." When he saw my father, he told him: "Zijo, motherfucker, who in the world brought you over here?" I don't know what my father answered, but then he ordered that man to be returned immediately to the room where he had been previously. And that's how they returned him to the room where he had been before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened later that night?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought him there about midnight. He was scared and he didn't talk much. He asked one of the people who were lying close to us for a cigarette. I think he was given a cigarette, and he lit a cigarette. I think someone brought something to drink. I can't remember whether it was water or tea. Anyway, after about one hour later, it was 1.00 in the morning, someone came to the door and called his name out again. I remember clearly that he stood up. He went to the door. He turned, looked at me, he smiled, and went out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see your father again?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you observed while you were in Omarska, did you see other people taken out and not returned to rooms?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many people who being taken off to be questioned. They would come back beaten badly. These interviews were mostly conducted during the day, and many of the people who were taken off for questioning at night never returned, and my father was among these people. He was taken from the room where I was, as I've described. I think Jasko Hrnic, Emir Karabasic, my neighbour, and my music teacher from elementary school, Nihad Jakupovic. That's as many people as I can remember now. There were more people than that, but it's just that now I can't remember. There were lots of persons I didn't know, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your other relatives that you've mentioned survive the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not around. They never returned. I can't really believe that they would still be alive after ten years. They are just not there, and their bodies were never found or identified. But once they were taken from Omarska, they never returned, and nothing more was heard of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware in early August of a visit of foreign journalists to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some journalists came. I did not see them myself. That day when they came, we had lunch in a hurry, my group. And at that time, I was staying in the white house for two or three days. So when the journalists came, we were in those rooms over there, unable to see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did things change after the foreign journalists visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After their first visit, no, nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall on the transfer of a large number of prisoners out of the camp around the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that day?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some confusion. There were many guards. They went around with lists. They called out names. They told people to go here and there according to those lists they had. They transferred people from one room to another, that sort of thing, but all based on the lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if they called out your father's name?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember clearly my father's name being called out. My cousins, too, Sakib Poljak and Sabid Poljak. I remember that clearly. I was glad in a way that they had been called out because that was a signal for me that they were still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see them again. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never again after the day they were taken off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after they called out all these lists of names and transferred people between rooms, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day when they went around with those lists and read out names, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used buses to take people away, most of the people. And late in the afternoon, perhaps about 5.00 or 6.00, I can't tell exactly, but all those people were driven out of the camp. Only the group in which I was stayed inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later learn where those people had been taken on the 7th of August, the prisoners that were driven out?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned, I think from the Red Cross, that a huge group was transferred to Manjaca and registered there by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if some of the prisoners were taken to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Manjaca and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners remained in the camp with you, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 150.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Omarska camp change, if at all, from that day, or the next day on?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those of us who stayed, we were really scared. We thought they had left us there to kill us. We all kept silent, more or less. We remained seated outside one of those buildings for a long time, and then late in the afternoon, they told us to go into a room, in which we then stayed. And no one touched us. There was some sort of a trough, a fountain. We could go out and drink water, use the toilet. They did not maltreat us, but still we were very scared. That same night, after midnight, I think it may have been around 2.00 or 3.00, early in the morning, you could hear lorries pulling over outside the building. And we thought they would kill us at that point. We were ordered to go out. Once we were out, they pulled the canvas of the lorry up and we saw, inside the lorry, mattresses, beds with mattresses. They told us to unload the mattresses and take them into the room in which we were staying. Those were bunk beds with iron frames. We did what they told us. We brought the beds into the room and we arranged them. We put the mattresses on the beds. Each of us was assigned a bed, and that was the first time in three months, approximately, that I got to lie down on a normal bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Omarska camp -- excuse me. Soon after the beds arrived, did you receive a visit from a foreign organisation?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, journalists came. The Red Cross did visit after about ten days, but I'm not sure now. I think we stayed for about 15 days after those other people had been transferred to Manjaca and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then just to be clear about, if I understand your answer, between the time the beds arrived and your transfer to Manjaca, foreign journalists and the International Red Cross visited the camp, is that correct, the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that Bernard Kouchner also came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bernard Kouchner?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kouchner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you remember the date that you were transferred to Omarska? If not, if you don't remember what the date was, if you don't remember, that's fine, that you were transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what month it was?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the Manjaca camp -- well, first, how long did you stay in the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until December 1992. I can't remember the date, but it was late December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Manjaca camp, did you see other prisoners from the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many people from Prijedor Municipality there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a very rough estimate of the percentage of the prisoners in Manjaca when you got there in August that were from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe about half of them were from Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In December, where were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a long time, there was talk of deportation from Manjaca, first to Croatia, and then to third countries. We were all convinced that we would be transferred at some point. We were receiving regular visits by the Red Cross, medical examinations. It was quite good as compared to Omarska. I think at one time, they even arranged -- they set a specific time when we were supposed to be transferred. But several days before that, they called out about 150 of us. They put us on to buses and transferred us to Bjeljina, Batkovici, without ever telling us that we would be transferred there to Bjeljina, Batkovici. We didn't know where we were going or what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After being in Batkovici -- by the way, can you tell us, is that in eastern Bosnia? Is that correct, northeastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's in northeastern Bosnia, some kilometres from Bjeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From December 1992 to the 9th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then exchanged in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when we were exchanged, near Turbet. It's a place name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the Omarska camp, did you receive -- did someone tell you or give you any paper saying that you were charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to be interrogated three times. And the third time I was taken there, some sort of indictment was handed to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what it charged you with?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it was something about armed rebellion, I think, setting up Kozarac Municipality, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you participated in any combat or any conflict, any fighting, up to that point?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they charged you with armed rebellion, had you been in any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. armed force? Had you fired a gun at anyone?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Territorial Defence for Jakupovici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has your father or any of your other relatives that you saw in the Omarska camp, have their bodies been exhumed, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have no information on that. We haven't learned anything about their bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from being given that one piece of paper, were you brought to court or were you involved in any proceedings regarding this allegation that you took part in an armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No court proceedings were ever initiated against me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions. Going back, you talked about when the large number of people were surrendering in Kozarac, you said goodbye to your mother and father and sister-in-law. Do you know from speaking to your father in the camp what happened to your family at that point?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to him about that. When they reached Kozarac, they were separated, men from women. My father was put on to a bus with other men and they were transferred to Omarska, while my mother, my sister-in-law and her baby boy, were transferred to the Trnopolje camp. They stayed in Trnopolje for a while. My mother had a sister who lived quite close to the camp, so they allowed them to leave the camp, and they went to her sister's house. And they stayed there for some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your mother and sister-in-law, then, leave the territory controlled by the SDS forces?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there for a while, a month or two. I can't remember. But then they joined a convoy for Gracanica, I think, by train.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the 1993, when you were -- have you been back to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never went back to Bosnia since I got out in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has anyone given you any information about the status of your family home and what has happened to that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother went there last year, and some of our neighbours had visited that area. That was even earlier. And we were given a number of photographs taken of our house and some video footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does your house look like now?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are just fragments of walls left standing. It's a ruin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poljak. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The floor is now for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Poljak. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. John Ostojic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Stakic before this Tribunal. I have a few questions for you. My examination will not be as long as the examination by the Prosecution. I know that it is difficult for you to testify about these events, but I ask you to muster enough strength to answer a few questions put by the Defence. Since we both speak the same language, although it's unnatural, please make a short pause after my question so that the interpreters have time to interpret what we are saying.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we begin?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will refer to some pages and lines in the transcript. This should not confuse you. I am doing so only for the record. Yesterday, on page 51 of the transcript, line 10 forward, you explained that you stopped going to school.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that schools continued operating after the takeover of power on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that most students got their certificates at the end of the school year without any problems?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know, please say that. Feel free to say it. That's an answer, too.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the following page of the transcript, you speak of a roadblock that was set up in Jakupovici. And you say that a tank broke through that barricade.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tank passed through that place, broke through or passed through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you assist us by telling us what the barricade was made of?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I know there were some logs, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when that barricade was set up?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that a trench had been dug next to the barricade?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a statement to investigators of the Prosecution on the 11th of January, 1996. Do you remember signing that statement?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like to ask the usher to just present this document to the witness so he can recognise his signature, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 1 at the bottom, on page 2 at the bottom, page 3, page 4, page 5, and on the last page, in the first half of the page, do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the representatives of the Tribunal, did you give statements to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was released from camp, when I was exchanged, I don't know how much time elapsed, but we gave a statement in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I would like the usher to give to the witness one statement. And I don't know whether you have these or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As usual, we don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honours. I have copies for Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, these documents were disclosed to you by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the OTP why we don't have these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: They are not offered by the Prosecution. They are not a statement taken by the Prosecution, nor were they used in our examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Respectfully, we disagree with this approach. As said earlier, this is not a pure common law system under our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and whenever there is an additional statement, this Trial Chamber wants to be provided with this additional material for better preparation. And may I ask the Defence, is there a translation into English of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I have ready translation copies as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the translation we also received from the OTP, so for the registrar and Their Honours. I apologise to His Honour Judge Fassi Fihri, but we have only this English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please give us five minutes or so that we can read it in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak, if you wish, you can also take the statement and read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak, you made this statement to a representative of the Office of the Centre of the Institute for the Investigation of Crimes against Humanity and International Law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made this statement in Zenica, but what the organisation was called, I can't remember. This is, however, my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, did you tell Enisa Poljak, a person who has the same last name as you, the truth?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this statement you say, underneath the part entitled "Statement," I quote: "At 14.10 hours on the 24th of May, 1992, in the village of Jakupovici, Prijedor Municipality, at the barricades that we had set up on the Banja Luka/Prijedor main road, the Yugoslav forces and Serb forces attacked our village." Do you remember having said this?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the barricade was on the main road linking Banja Luka and Prijedor? Would you repeat your reply because it has not been interpreted.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then go on to say: "Outnumbered and outgunned by the enemy, we were not able to stop their forces from breaking into our village. My neighbour, Jakupovic, also known as Jakupa, whose first name was Enis, was killed. There were some wounded people, too. So we had to retreat into the village in order to evacuate the civilian population to Kozarac." Do you remember having said this?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand this correctly, that from this checkpoint or barricade, you also retreated?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was making this statement, I was talking about most people, but the entire village was not at the barricade. It's just how it sounds because of the words I used. I was relating what had happened in general to all the inhabitants of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people participated in total, I mean all who did shifts at this checkpoint or this barricade, if you know? How many people from Jakupovici participated in guard duty, manning the barricade?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barricade? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we agree, however, that all those who manned the barricade were of Bosniak ethnicity, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you retreated from Jakupovici, you went in the direction of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the conflict in Jakupovici and Kozarac broke out, did you ever go to Kozarac after the takeover of power on the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go from Jakupovici to Kozarac between the 30th of April and May, between the 30th of April and the 4th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that day, but I can't remember for sure. On that day when there was shooting, or perhaps the day before, we had a horse, a horse-drawn cart. And my brother, he was married to a woman from Brdjani. So we loaded some flour and oil and other staples, and my father told me to take it to those relatives, those in-laws there, so that we would have it there if we had to flee from our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you see armed men in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To go to Brdjani, you don't have to go through Kozarac. I took the old road from Jakupovici via Babici, Kustici [phoen], Kamicani, and Softici to Brdjani. So I did not go to Kozarac at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out and you arrived in Kozarac --

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Brdjani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Brdjani. Did you enter Kozarac at all?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't enter Kozarac at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Brdjani, did you see trenches that had been dug?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't move around a lot, but I didn't see anything around the house where I went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, or later on, did you learn that the first vehicle in the column of military vehicles, a member of the JNA was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. killed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the conflict, was there one column moving in the direction of Jakupovici, I mean a military column, or were there two? And can you tell us from what direction they were coming? Were they coming from Banja Luka or from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I apologise, but I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is probably too vague. I will try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a military column was moving in the direction of Jakupovici, which is why a request was made that the barricade be removed from the main road?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a piece of news on Radio Prijedor at about 1.00 p.m. on that day. I was sitting down at the table having lunch and listening to the radio, and I heard this news item saying that unless the barricade was removed, it would be removed by force or attacked, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know, then, from what direction the military column came?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From where the attack was carried out?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an attack. There was an attack, and it came from the direction of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you to concentrate on the point in time when you separated from your parents. You said that you set out in the direction of Kozara, that there were people all around, women, children, elderly people. We are speaking of the time when a surrender was negotiated, the surrender of the people from Kozarac. Were there a lot of people outside, outdoors, on that occasion, in the streets, around the houses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the shooting stop then?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we could still hear the shooting. I'm not -- well, I didn't think about it at the time. I was thinking about where I should go, what I should do, how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there shelling?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that a group of armed Muslims led by Kemal Alagic, whose nickname was Divljak, carried out a counterattack on Kozarac immediately before Kozarac was taken by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. Even the name, I've never heard the name before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the people who retreated in the direction of Kozara with you, have you ever heard any reference to a group known as "Kola's group"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about Kola's group, but I don't think those people were with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were members of Ramiz's group among you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please excuse me, but my sister-in-law's brother and I were alone, we set out alone. And then we spent the nights in the woods there, and in the morning when we woke up, there were many people there. This was not a group --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise if the question was not sufficiently clear. I did not infer for a moment that you, yourself, were a member of either Kola's or Ramiz's group. I am merely asking you whether there was any reference at the time to any members of those two groups being among you. Can you please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there among you, perhaps, Mr. Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness has already said that he was alone together with the sister. This is extremely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell us, to the best of your knowledge, how many checkpoints there were in Jakupovici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know of the barricade on the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people who went with you in the direction of Kozara, you say that some of them were armed and some were even wearing camouflage uniform. Did they bring those weapons with them from Kozarac, from Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How in the world should I know where they took those weapons?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Just one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poljak. The Defence has no further questions for you at this point.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Fassi Fihri, any questions? No questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify one point. Re-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the attack you learned came on Jakupovici came from the direction of Banja Luka, as I understood it. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if we had S51, the map, brought -- put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us on that map where the barricade was, and from what you learned, what direction the attack came, the tank that attacked.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barricade was perhaps here. I can't see here -- I think this is the road linking Jakupovici and Kevljani. The barricade was here somewhere and the attack was carried out from the direction of Banja Luka, this road here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So just for the record, the witness indicated the red line just above the dot marked "D. Jakupovici" and indicated on the map that the attack came from the right, the area marked "Banja Luka." No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But then for clarification purposes, is it the intention of the Defence to tender the presented documents as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I think that we have on the transcript everything that is needed, and the witness confirmed his statement. So it's not our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Just for clarification, that never reference can be made, especially to the second part of this document, later on because in case you should have questions as regards the two last sentences of this statement given there, you have to do it now because we can't summon the witness once again for these purposes, and no inferences may be drawn from these two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have that intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of this contribution, any further remarks by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then for the record, these documents are not tendered, and therefore not admitted into evidence. We have to thank you for coming, and not only for coming, also for giving your testimony under these very difficult circumstances for you. We all know how difficult it is for you to recall these events at that time. And we just can say thank you for coming and giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness is excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it possible to have 10 or 15 minutes to set up for the next witness. I asked her to bring some graphics with her, and also there's some exhibits which have not yet arrived which I plan to use with her. Just for the Court's information, those were 65 ter numbers 4 -- number 7, number 412, and number 436. I believe the witness is, I believe, in the witness room. We could start but I would prefer 10 minutes to just go over with her how we're going to present the graphics and get the exhibits down here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for giving us these exhibit numbers in due time. And we'll take the opportunity and find these documents also for our preparation. The trial stays adjourned for the next 20 minutes. This brings us to, say, 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for everyone's information, I asked that copies be brought down for everyone, so if you don't have those with you, those 65 ters, they will be here in a few minutes. --- Break taken at 11.11 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. We can expect as to the fact that we can read the documents a short representation or presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think -- I would estimate the direct examination will be about a half hour, just to remind the Court, I believe I stated this before in Court, Ms. Tabeau is in the process of updating the report that Your Honours have that was prepared for the Keraterm case, specifically regarding the numbers and characteristics of those who went missing or are known to have been killed in the Prijedor Municipality in 1992. And that will not be ready until after the break, at least, it may be disclosed before the break or during the break but she will not be prepared to testify on that until after the summer break. But in this report, she also talks about demographic changes in the municipality, and that would be the subject of her testimony today, simply the demographic changes in the municipality, and it's really beginning -- it would be the figures 1, table 2 on page 7 of the English version of the report, figures 1, table 2, figure 2, table 3, and figure 3 of those statistical results. The documents, the 65 ter documents, are the census for Bosnia, the 1991 census. That's 65 ter number 7. 65 ter number 412 is an article that appeared in Kozarski Vjesnik in 1993 regarding a census conducted in Prijedor. And the final one, which is 436, 436 is a census or information on the number and ethnic structure of the population in the various municipalities in the area of the Banja Luka state security department. This was dated 1995, was part of the seizures from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. This morning, I forgot one issue. Of course, it's also for this case of high relevance whether or not the case Prosecutor versus Mr. Mrdja can really be heard during a break of this case. And I would ask you to inform us as soon as possible on the development in this case. You may remember I requested the parties in that case to give us in writing whether or not they are prepared to start the case the 1st of October until Wednesday next week, which of course is the ultimate possible day. In case there should be a problem, then we should stop one hour earlier with this case one or other day next week, in order to have an additional status conference in the other case that we know where we are and we can prepare the necessary documents or not by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can give Your Honour the information I have right now. I've talked to the higher ups in my office. It's simply a matter of finding personnel to conduct the necessary searches for Rule 68 and the discovery. They have told me that they will find someone to do that. It hasn't been assigned yet, but I think the answer that we will have is yes, we will be ready by the 1st of October. We will have all of the disclosures done in time and the Rule 68 done in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please, also contact the Defence counsel that we know what's going on. And I think it's only fair that the Defence knows in advance, if possible already before the Court recess, what's going on in September and October. Thank you for this. And the usher may bring in Madam Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Tabeau. You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And the Office of the Prosecutor may start the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, can you please tell us, who are you employed by at the present time? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I'll repeat my question. But before I do, let me remind you that our conversation, although taking place in English, will be translated into French and B/C/S so we both need to speak slowly and pause between the question and the answer. Can you tell the Court, who are you employed by at the present time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm employed by the Office of the Prosecutor. I am a demographer there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have been working approximately two years now. Since September 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what specifically are your duties with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My responsibilities include estimating demographic consequences of the conflict in the Former Yugoslavia, in particular, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When doing this, I work with a group of other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where you received your university education and in what field?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I graduated in statistics and econometrics, obtaining a master's degree in statistics and econometrics from the Warsaw School of Economics, which is the major economic university in Poland, in Warsaw. I originally come from Poland. Shortly afterwards, I started to work at the university as an academic teacher. I taught statistics and elements of demography to undergraduate courses at the Warsaw School of Economics. And also worked at that time on a Ph.D. project that I completed successfully eight years later and obtained a Ph.D. degree in mathematical demography. My field of discipline of my Ph.D. is mortality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Dr. Tabeau, is it correct that you received your Ph.D. then from Warsaw University?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, it is Warsaw School of Economics, Warsaw University, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you're testifying in English. Are you conversant in any other languages?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I speak, of course, Polish. This is my native tongue. I speak Russian, German and Dutch, and English is just one of these languages. Since 1991, I have been here in the Netherlands. I arrived here to work on a project with Dutch demographers in the Dutch National Demographic Institute. I stayed there ten years approximately working, again, in the field of mortality. I was responsible then in that institute for mortality projections that I made for many European countries, the Netherlands and other countries of the European union, Spain, France, United Kingdom, Norway, many, many countries. And I also worked on projects about demographic aspects of the situation in Poland, for instance, Czech Republic. So I have knowledged or demography, say, more specifically of mortality issues in different types of countries, western and non-western countries, European countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You skipped ahead a little bit from my question, but going back to it for a moment, I'm going to talk about the languages. You did answer the languages that you are conversant in. But, specifically, you mentioned Russian. Are you able to read Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I am able to read Cyrillic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your knowledge of Polish and Russian, do you have any ability to work at all in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I know a little bit B/C/S as well. I followed a course of B/C/S here at the Tribunal, but it is the same group of languages, Slavic languages, so I can understand to a certain extent. I am not fluent, no way, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about your work experience, and I just want to make sure we haven't missed anything. After getting your Ph.D., did you go directly to Holland? What did you do after receiving your Ph.D. from the Warsaw University?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I came directly to Holland. It was in 1991 that I received my Ph.D., and directly afterwards, I came here. And first was invited to work an a three-year project that later continued in the form of new projects in the same institute, Dutch National Demographic Institute. So it all together took approximately ten years that I worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please pause -- allow a short pause before you answer so that the interpreters can catch up. In that Dutch National Demographic Institute, you said you worked on mortality. And is it correct you worked on mortality in other European countries? How wide was the area of countries that you worked on? Did it include only western countries or what countries were included?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I worked on western countries, but occasionally also on Eastern European and central European countries like Poland, for instance, Czech Republic, Hungary. These are the same group of countries -- it is a comparable group of countries to, I think, the Former Yugoslavia. Demographics in these countries show similar patterns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Going now to the report that you prepared, or excuse me, the report that I have in front of me entitled "Population Changes in Prijedor from 1991 to 1997" by Helge Brunborg, Torkild Lyngstad - excuse my pronunciation - and Ewa Tabeau, dated the 19th of April, 2001, research report prepared for the case of the Keraterm camp IT-95-8, is it correct that, as dated, that this report was prepared in April of 2001, finalised?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The report was finalised by that time, but the project resulting in this report started much earlier, approximately 1998. It was Helge Brunborg, the demographer previously employed at the Office of the Prosecutor, who started this project. And I arrived in September 2000, joined Torkild Lyngstad, who was assistant, demographic assistant at the time, and we finished this project by writing this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this report discusses changes in the population and the ethnic percentages in Prijedor from before the conflict and after the conflict, but then also discusses the number of persons missing or killed in the municipality and the characteristics of that group of persons? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the data that has become available to you regarding the missing and dead since this report was finalised, has additional information become available to the demographic unit of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We acquired new sources, extensive sources, and received, for instance, a more recent version of the list of missing persons, ICRC list of missing persons. So the sources that we have now at our disposal are much more extensive and much more reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have there been exhumations since this report was prepared, and the data of those exhumations, has that become available to you between then and the present time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, we received new information from the exhumation projects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you also received access to a database regarding declarations of death in the Bosnian courts since this report was prepared?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, we also received access to these databases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given this new information, is it correct that you have been asked by myself to update the portions of this report regarding the total number killed and missing and the characteristics of that group, and that that report is in progress?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, we simply want to discuss, then, the data that -- regarding the changes in the population, pre and post conflict and the ethnic composition of the municipality of Prijedor. Doctor, going to your report, is it correct that data that you used in your report include censuses conducted in the Former Yugoslavia in 1971, 1981, and 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what information you have about those censuses and your professional judgement regarding the reliability of the data that was collected?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The population census is the most complete and reliable source of information about the population, about demographic aspects of the population, and also many other aspects, economic aspects, for instance. The censuses you mentioned and also all the censuses that are discussed in the report were all conducted by the authorities, statistical authorities, of the Former Yugoslavia who, as is the practice in all other countries, certainly followed, to a large degree, international guidelines regarding the way the census should be conducted. As far as my knowledge is considered, I know more about the population census from 1991 than about other censuses. But taking this census as an example, I can say that this is a census that is certainly in line with international guidelines and practice of other countries. I myself participated as an interviewer during my university education in one of the population censuses in Poland, so I know exactly how the practical part of the census looks like. And from the documentation I have about the census, 1991 census, for the Former Yugoslavia, Bosnia and Herzegovina in particular, I can see that all necessary requirements have been fulfilled, necessary instructions had been returned and provided to people conducting the census. The questionnaire is just a standard questionnaire. Questions are explained in a very exhaustive and specific way in the instructions. So from this point of view, I must say that the preparation of the census, the census questionnaire, and I believe the way the census was conducted, all these satisfies the requirements in such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you in a moment to describe how it was actually conducted in your knowledge. But perhaps preceding that, we need to explain, is there something called a - forgive my pronunciation - maticni broj in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Maticni broj is a personal identification number that was introduced in the Former Yugoslavia in the early 1980s. And since then, it has been in use also in population censuses. It was also used in the latest census, 1991 census. It is a unique identification number issued to every citizen of the country that is reported on that census questionnaire and can be used later to identify persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how that number is constructed and whether it contains any information about the individual?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is a long number consisting of several digits. Part of this number is information about the date of birth of a particular individual and the municipality, as far as I remember, of birth. Coded, of course, it is not the name that is included in the number. So also some digits are reserved to code the sex of the person and the general region the person was resident of at the moment the number was issued, given to the person. It is just a combination of certain strings of characters that inform in a coded way about who is this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that fact that this number includes information about the date or, at least, year of birth of the individual, their area of residence and sex, is that useful to you in your demographic work in matching individuals and different times periods?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The date of birth is complete. It is not year, but also day and month. It is extremely important that we have this information included in maticni broj. While matching records from the census to other sources, we can compare the strings that we understand the meaning of, and perfectly -- be perfectly clear about whether records are the same or not in the different sources. Yes, it is essential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us exactly how in practice the census was conducted. Was something mailed to households? How was the census of 1991 conducted, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The census, as far as I know, was conducted by interviewers who visited every household in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm speaking now about Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I believe it was the same for the whole country for the Former Yugoslavia. The interviewers questioned households. Households were represented usually by head of households who was giving answers regarding every member of the household. It was a direct interview. This was the method. And the census, of course, took some time, say, approximately one month. It is a very huge survey, population census. Knowing that the population at that time, 1991, was approximately 4.4 million individuals, it is understandable that the census cannot be completed within one day. It takes some time. But in official statistics, there is one date taken as the moment of that census. I think it's the last day of March in this case, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of information about the individuals residing in the household was obtained? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Census questionnaire is a very complex questionnaire. It consists of several pages. Part of this information are personal details about individuals: Names, place of birth, date of birth, of course. In fact, we have questions about education of persons, professional activity, occupation. We have questions about many, many other aspects, including ownership of certain property types and tools, et cetera, et cetera. This is a very complex questionnaire. For us, the part including personal details and socioeconomic information about individuals was most essential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the census, were individuals asked or given an opportunity or asked to identify their ethnicity, and if so, in the 1991 census, can you tell us what the categories were, how the ethnicity was recorded?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Ethnicity and religion were included in the census. Ethnicity is always in these type of surveys an open question, so there are no suggested responses. And every individual is free to report what he or she thinks he is. So people identify themselves by giving answers that they belong to one ethnic group. That was the case, of course, in the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the data was collected, were those ethnicities put into groups?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The original responses were just individual responses. Any ethnicity could be reported, and many were reported: Muslim ethnicity, Serb, Croat, Montenegro, Hungarian, Norwegian and Polish. So ethnicity and nationality sometimes were given as possible answers. For our work, it is not very informative to work with a very large list of items informing about ethnicities. In that census, it is necessary to group the items in a certain way, in a way that would make it possible for us to summarise the information about the ethnic composition of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have 65 ter Exhibit Number 7. I'd like to proffer that as an exhibit and have it be given the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be S227, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps one could be given to the witness, also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S227.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, showing you S227, can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, this is a list. The first column includes the names of municipalities starting from the left, and then we have the geographic area in square kilometres. Then we have the number of the population, total, I believe. And then numbers of the population for ethnic groups, starting with Croats, then Muslims, Serbs, Yugoslavs, and others. And the table is continued. There are two parts of this table. In the second part, we see the same headings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, another piece of paper is being handed out. I thought it was a translation, but on closer examination I see it's not. I'm just checking to see. Apparently, it's supposed to be a translation, although I see that the square metres of the municipality is not included in the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I think that the municipalities are listed in different order. I do not believe this is a translation. It's obviously not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going to S227, the one that's in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Having a look on this document in B/C/S as from 1991, unfortunately, especially when it comes to Prijedor, one can't read the last column. Probably we can be provided with a better photocopy later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, on S227, is it correct that Prijedor is listed just above the midpoint of the page? It's a very bad copy, very small print. In addition to the 1991 census, you had access to the 1971 and 1981 censuses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. We had access to certain publications reporting summary statistics from the censuses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These results were published by the federal authorities in Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding Prijedor, did you prepare in your report on page 7 of the English version -- I'd like now to talk about particularly table 2. And do you have a copy of that to put on the ELMO? Okay. In the page in front of us, we have both figure 1 and table 2. I'd like to first talk to you about table number 2 so perhaps we could focus in on that, the lower half of the page. And that's also in the report, so we can follow along.
